title: Point mutations in the FimH lectin domain: predicted folding stability versus conformational dynamics for R60P, Q133K and Y137A
summary: Background. The adhesin FimH attaches uropathogenic Escherichia coli to the urinary epithelium through a force-regulated catch-bond that single lectin-domain substitutions can modulate. How such substitutions reshape the dynamics of the isolated lectin domain, and whether stability predictors anticipate them, is unclear. Methods. We compared the wild-type (WT) lectin domain (PDB 4XO8, apo) with R60P, Y137A and Q133K, using three 500 ns molecular dynamics (MD) replicates per system (6 microseconds total) and three folding-stability predictors (FoldX, a Cartesian-ddG-type Rosetta protocol, ERIS-2). The replicate was the unit of analysis (n = 3), with 95% confidence intervals and a WT replicate-to-replicate control. Results. FoldX and ERIS-2 ranked the variants consistently, R60P most destabilising and Q133K neutral; the Rosetta value for Q133K was anomalously high. All systems stayed folded. R60P gave the only reproduced local change, loss of beta-strand structure at residues 60-61 and of three local hydrogen bonds. Y137A did not bring Thr158 into the pocket, and the Q133K Gln133-Asp54 polar contact became a Lys133-Asp54 salt bridge. In the principal-component landscape, departures from the WT region came from individual replicates (Y137A replicate 1; Q133K replicates 2-3), not a systematic shift. Conclusions. A substitution perturbs local structure most clearly when it breaks a beta-strand (R60P), and the stability predictions and dynamics together give a consistent ranking of the variants, including the first dynamic characterisation of Q133K. The results characterise the apo lectin domain and give a reproducible basis for interpreting FimH mutations, not for inferring affinity. Keywords: FimH; lectin domain; point mutations; molecular dynamics; folding stability ({Delta}{Delta}G); protein stability prediction; principal component analysis; urinary tract infection.

title: Conformational heterogeneity and state-dependent stability of active-site loops in Trametes versicolor laccase
summary: How can a single active site accept substrates that differ widely in size, shape and charge? We have addressed this question for the fungal laccase from Trametes versicolor, a promiscuous multicopper oxidase, by mapping the conformational ensemble of the substrate-free (but fully copper-loaded) enzyme. Combining 50 s of unbiased atomistic molecular dynamics seeded through tICA-metadynamics with a variational autoencoder and VAMPnets, we resolve a set of metastable states that differ mainly in the conformations of the two loops, L1 (G159-L164) and L2 (F332-F337), lining the substrate binding pocket. The loops interconvert on the sub-millisecond timescale, and their rearrangement is accompanied by an extensive rewiring of the hydrogen-bond network well beyond the active site. Conformations from our earlier dye-bound simulations map onto specific regions of this landscape, showing that the bound poses correspond to conformations that the free enzyme already visits. A correlation network connecting the two loops passes through the protein region surrounding the T1 copper and singles out T114, the residue with the highest betweenness centrality along the path. Nonequilibrium alchemical calculations show that T114A destabilizes the five states by very different amounts, between 3.2 and 8.2 kcal/mol relative to a common peptide reference, with the largest penalties occurring in states carrying a persistent T114-D118 hydrogen bond. A single side chain interaction, located away from the substrate-binding contacts, thus offers a handle for tuning the conformational balance of the active site, and this prediction can be tested directly by mutagenesis.

title: Interactions with lipid membrane modulate the conformational dynamics and energy landscape of Tumor Necrosis Factor
summary: Tumor Necrosis Factor (TNF) is a trimeric cytokine that exists in soluble (sTNF) and membrane-bound (mTNF) forms, both of which regulate immune responses through interactions with their cognate receptors. sTNF has been the subject of extensive biophysical investigations, leading to a prevailing mechanistic model in which a symmetric arrangement of the trimer promotes receptor signaling, whereas asymmetric conformations inhibit this function. In contrast, the structural and energetic landscape of mTNF remains largely under-explored. Here, we combined multi-microsecond unbiased molecular dynamics and Metadynamics-Adaptive Biasing Force simulations to characterize mTNF embedded in a heterogeneous lipid bilayer. We show that in the absence of membrane engagement, the extracellular domain (ECD) dynamically samples multiple asymmetric conformations similar to those observed in sTNF. The association of the ECD with the membrane, mediated primarily by the basic residues R78-R82, R107, R108, R120, and R207, restricts conformational heterogeneity and stabilizes the symmetric state. By quantifying the ECD-membrane interactions, we demonstrate that the symmetric state in the membrane-bound ECD is stabilized over asymmetric conformations to a greater extent than in sTNF. This energetic effect, together with the spatial confinement imposed by the lipid bilayer, may explain the previously observed reduced affinity of certain biologics for mTNF. In conclusion, our work elucidates how the membrane influences the structure, dynamics, and energetics of TNF. These mechanistic insights could guide future efforts to design mTNF-selective inhibitors that account for both membrane constraints and the energetic modulation of the ECD conformational landscape.

title: Pleckstrin Homology-based proximity-labeling reveal lipid-associated interactomes
summary: Phosphoinositides (PIPs) organize membrane-associated signaling, but the proteins associated with specific PIPs and their regulation remain poorly characterized. Here, we establish a lipid-binding domain-based proximity-labeling approach to map PIP-associated proteomes in vivo, and applied it to plant cells. We identify distinct protein networks associated with PI4P and PI(4,5)P2, linking these lipids to membrane signaling, transport, and organization. Using molecular dynamics simulations and in vivo validation we further reveal how two previously uncharacterized PIP effectors, ALTERED RESPONSE TO GRAVITY-LIKE1 (ARL1) and HYPERSENSITIVE RESPONSE 1 (HIR1), engage with PIPs to regulate their membrane localization and nanodomain organization. Finally, we outline how PIP-associated proteomes change in response to prominent abiotic stress conditions, including salt and heat, in Arabidopsis. Our work establishes a platform for investigating lipid-associated proteomes in vivo and reveals how PIP-specific and stress-responsive protein networks contribute to membrane organization and cellular responses.

title: Forecasting viral antigenic evolution from phylogenetic trees
summary: Forecasting the evolution of viral proteins can help inform pandemic preparedness and guide the development of interventions. Phylogenetic trees provide historical records of pathogen evolution, which are key for retrospective analysis, but using them to predict future genotypic changes remains challenging. We introduce antiGen, a machine learning model that learns from the evolutionary past of viruses to forecast the evolutionary future. antiGen achieves state-of-the-art performance in forecasting SARS-CoV-2 spike protein mutations according to a variety of metrics, including the prediction of mutations in the receptor binding domain, mutations never previously seen, and mutations with high prevalence. Most experimentally tested antiGen-forecasted spike variants retain pseudoviral infectivity in vitro, supporting their functional plausibility. Evaluations on surface proteins of influenza virus, respiratory syncytial virus, and dengue virus further demonstrate applicability across viruses with differing amounts of available sequencing data. Finally, we develop a model trained across 49 viral proteins from 27 viruses, which improves forecasting performance over models trained on individual protein phylogenies. Together, these results support learning from phylogenetic histories as an approach to model viral amino acid changes prospectively, with applications in epidemiology and therapeutic development.

title: Evaluating Temporal Genomic Data for Detecting and Characterizing Balancing Selection
summary: Balancing selection encompasses a diverse set of evolutionary mechanisms that maintain genetic polymorphism within populations. However, both detecting balancing selection and distinguishing among its underlying mechanisms remain challenging. Recent advances in the generation of temporal genetic data and the application of machine learning offer new opportunities to address these challenges. In this study, we tested whether temporal genetic data improve the detection of balancing selection and the discrimination between two major balancing selection mechanisms, overdominance and negative frequency-dependent selection. Using forward simulations, we summarized temporal genetic data with features derived from a diverse set of population genetic summary statistics and trained support vector machine and random forest classifiers. Temporal data substantially improved the discrimination of balancing selection from neutral evolution, particularly when summarized by the first four moments of each statistic across time, increasing accuracy by up to 10%. Among individual summary statistics, simple measures of genetic diversity unexpectedly outperformed several more sophisticated statistics. In contrast, summary statistic-based approaches remained insufficient for effectively distinguishing overdominance from negative frequency-dependent selection, even when temporal information was incorporated. These results demonstrate the value of temporal genetic data for detecting balancing selection while highlighting the limitations of summary statistic-based inference for resolving alternative balancing selection mechanisms.

title: Deep sequence-function mapping reveals computationally unpredictable epistatic trajectories that drive laboratory evolution
summary: The black-box nature of directed evolution has been constraining advances in enzyme engineering and the wider application of engineered biocatalysts. While conventional deep sequence-function mapping has delivered insights into sequence space architecture, it lacks the ability to analyse adaptive landscapes and fully grasp the long-term impact of epistasis on the accessibility of evolutionary trajectories. Here, we introduce Deep Evolutionary Trajectory Mapping (dETM) which tracks the winners of a multi-round evolutionary campaign to map catalytic rates across the adaptive landscape of an imine reductase. We identified founder variants as stepping stones towards fitness peaks and recognise positive epistasis as their competitive advantage over alternative lineages. State-of-the-art machine learning models could not predict the resulting winning trajectories, which highlights the importance of decoding design principles for successful evolution experimentally. Permissive selection and ultrahigh-throughput screening emerge as foundations of derisking landscape traversal by keeping multiple paths accessible and avoiding diminishing returns.

title: Evaluating the ability of spatial transcriptomics foundation models to learn multi-scale spatial variation
summary: Spatial gene expression results from the superposition of multiple sources of variation in gene expression across different spatial scales, including local microenvironment-associated variation and global spatial gradients. Spatial foundation models (SFMs) are large-scale machine learning models trained on cohorts of spatial transcriptomics (ST) data that, in principle, learn the different sources of spatial variation in gene expression. However, the embeddings learned by SFMs are difficult to interpret, and it remains unclear whether they fully capture such spatial variation. Here, we develop SAFFRON, a sparse autoencoder (SAE)-based framework for interpreting and evaluating SFMs. SAFFRON uses a Matryoshka SAE to decompose dense SFM embeddings into sparse, human-interpretable features and evaluates whether these features correlate with known sources of spatial variation. Using SAFFRON, we systematically benchmark the ability of several recent SFMs to identify local and global spatial variation in gene expression. We find that only two SFMs learn global spatial gradients more accurately than naive, non-foundation model baselines; further investigating one such SFM, SAFFRON reveals that these gradients are concentrated in a small subset of sparse, human-interpretable SAE features. On the other hand, no SFM learns local patterns (A{beta} plaque microenvironment-associated patterns) more accurately than such baselines. Our findings suggest that current SFMs do not systematically learn multi-scale spatial variation in gene expression. Code: SAFFRON is available at https://github.com/chitra-lab/SAFFRON.

title: VF Mutations Lock JAK2 and TYK2 Kinase Dimers in a More Stable Conformation: Molecular Dynamics Reveals Enhanced Interface Rigidity
summary: Homologous oncogenic valine-to-phenylalanine (VF) mutations, JAK2V617F and TYK2V678F, are key drivers of constitutive JAK/STAT signaling and pathogenesis of myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs) and rare TYK2 associated hematologic disorders. However, their atom-level mechanisms and divergent structural impacts remain poorly defined, hindering precision therapeutic development. Here, we conducted 4 X 100 ns all atom simulation; 100 ns all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to systematically compare dimer stability and interfacial interaction networks between wild-type and VF mutant JAK2/TYK2. Both VF mutations significantly enhanced dimer stability by increasing the abundance and persistence of inter-monomer hydrogen bonds and salt bridges. The VF mutants also increased electrostatic complementarity at the PK_PK interface and induced novel stabilizing inter chain contacts involving FERM domains. Consistent with this, MM/PBSA binding free energy calculations confirmed stronger energetic preference for dimerization in TYK2V678F, while JAK2V617F conferred only moderate stabilization. Collectively, our findings uncover how homologous oncogenic mutations drive distinct structural and energetic consequences across JAK paralogs, directly linking mutation-specific dimer stabilization to aberrant signaling in MPNs and rare hematologic diseases. on to aberrant signaling in MPNs and rare hematologic diseases.

title: Machine Learning-Enhanced Mucosal Luminal Interface Metaproteomics Reveals Diagnostic Potential of Microbial Proteins in Pediatric Inflammatory Bowel Disease
summary: Abstract: Background: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD), a chronic gastrointestinal disorder with two main subtypes, Crohn's Disease (CD) and Ulcerative Colitis (UC), is associated with more aggressive phenotypes and greater diagnostic complexity in pediatric patients. Conventional diagnostic biomarkers, lack sufficient distinguishing power between IBD subtypes. This study aimed to investigate and compare proteomic and metaproteomic profiles of pediatric IBD (PIBD) patients and healthy controls to develop a diagnostic panel capable of accurately diagnose IBD and distinguish its subtypes. Methods: We performed an in-depth evaluation of mucosal luminal interface samples from PIBD patients and healthy individuals, separately analyzing both the human proteome and microbial metaproteome data. The study involved selecting appropriate protein sets, employing feature selection techniques and machine learning across three intestinal regions: the terminal ileum, ascending colon, and descending colon. Results: Notably, panels composed solely of microbial biomarkers outperformed both human-only and combined human-microbial panels, achieving highly accurate results. Furthermore, the ascending colon emerged as the optimal sampling site, a result that aligns with the rich microbial diversity revealed in its taxonomic profile. Conclusions: Using a machine learning-based strategy on combined proteomics and metaproteomics, this study uncovered disease-relevant signaling pathways and delivered taxonomic as well as functional insights into the microbial dysbiosis of PIBD. A diagnostic panel built around microbial proteins (particularly those originating from the ascending colon) emerges as a promising tool for more precise stratification of PIBD subtypes. Larger, prospective studies are now needed to validate these candidate biomarkers and translate them into clinically deployable diagnostic panels. Keywords: Metaproteome, Biomarker, Pediatric Inflammatory bowel disease, Machine learning, Mucosal luminal interface.

title: Multimodal conformational landscape and thermodynamics of coupled folding and binding in an intrinsically disordered protein region
summary: Intrinsically disordered proteins and peptides, as well as flexible protein regions, often bind folded protein partners through coupled folding and binding, but the underlying conformational landscapes and thermodynamics remain challenging to resolve. The large conformational space of the unbound molecule and its interactions with the folded partner make it difficult to identify and efficiently sample the slow collective motions governing association and folding. Here, we use enhanced-sampling molecular dynamics to investigate the coupled binding and folding of the intrinsically disordered region of FCP1 phosphatase upon interaction with the folded transcription factor Rap74, a process that modulates the activity of RNA polymerase II. OneOPES enhanced sampling simulations reveal a multimodal binding landscape comprising native, flipped and disordered-bound states, and identify hydrophobic contacts as early determinants of association followed by progressive helix formation. Circuit topology analysis further elucidates the FCP1 folding mechanism by identifying a characteristic topological transition accompanying helix formation and its stabilisation upon binding. To resolve the thermodynamics of the process, we introduce Divide et impera, a thermodynamic decomposition that separates the free-energy cost of folding from the binding free energy of the folded conformation. This approach reduces the conformational complexity of individual calculations while preserving the thermodynamic connection between unbound and bound states, enabling the calculation of absolute binding free energies in close agreement with experiment. These results establish a framework for connecting conformational heterogeneity, binding mechanisms and thermodynamics in coupled folding and binding of disordered proteins, with potential applications in the rational design and development of peptide therapeutics.

title: Extensive SARS-CoV-2 spike sequence diversification converges on a bounded, low-dimensional physicochemical space
summary: During the COVID-19 pandemic, SARS-CoV-2 accumulated extensive amino acid variation in its spike protein. However, the extent to which sequence diversification translates into physicochemical diversity remains unclear. Here, we analyzed 271,769 unique spike protein sequences from 12 geographical regions using three physicochemical descriptors: net charge at pH 7.0, hydropathy, and aliphatic index. To characterize temporal changes in physicochemical space, we compared the squared Mahalanobis distances of observed sequences with those of Monte Carlo-simulated sequences containing randomized amino acid substitutions, constrained to the number of empirically variable positions. We applied trimmed clustering to characterize sequence distributions in physicochemical space and used Shannon entropy to assess spatiotemporal relationships between genotypic and physicochemical diversity across geographic regions. Empirical physicochemical displacement increased early in the observation period and subsequently stabilized, despite continued increases in variable amino acid positions and accumulated substitutions. In contrast, simulated trajectories exhibited greater and sustained physicochemical divergence. Trimmed clustering identified six distinct physicochemical groups repeatedly occupied by genetically divergent lineages differing in mutation burden, amino acid composition, and emergence time. Shannon entropy analyses revealed broadly similar nonlinear temporal patterns across geographic regions, with differences between genotypic and physicochemical entropy tending to be negative. These findings indicate that extensive spike protein sequence diversification occurred within a comparatively restricted physicochemical space, consistent with a many-to-one relationship between amino acid sequences and physicochemical states. This framework provides a quantitative approach for investigating physicochemical constraints on viral protein evolution and may inform future machine learning approaches to epitope prediction and vaccine antigen design.

title: Evolutionary Stratification of Codon Usage Bias In Plants Arises from GC3 Composition and Translational Optimization
summary: Codon usage bias is a fundamental genomic characteristic that prefers non-random preferential use of synonymous codons. It is a major determinant of translational efficiency, gene regulation, and molecular evolution. However, the evolutionary bias and functional relevance of codon usage bias across the plant lineage is poorly defined and yet to understand what are the major factors responsible for relative synonymous codon usage (RSCU) in genomes and how codon usage bias influences the gene regulation, molecular evolution genomes. A genome-wide codon usage bias study of coding DNA sequences of 262 plant genome was conducted. It encompassed more than 4.6 billion codons from > 11 million coding sequences. Relative synonymous codon usage, codon adaptation index, codon-anticodon mapping, effective number of codon (ENC)-GC3, GC1,2-GC3, parity rule 2 (PR2-bias), molecular economy, and machine learning approaches were used for the study. It was found that codon usage bias was strongly non-random and exhibited a clear phylogenetic structuring. The higher plants favoured A/T-ending, whereas early-diverging lineages were enriched in G/C-ending codons. Analysis of RSCU, codon adaptation index, and codon-anticodon pairing indicated that translational selection is mediated by tRNA availability, contributing sustainability to these molecular patterns. Machine-learning approaches identified a small subset of codons having outsized influence on genome-wide codon usage landscapes. Further studies revealed the presence of robust inverse relationships between the effective number of codons and GC content at synonymous third positions. Neutrality analysis revealed approximately 61% of variation was driven by mutational pressure, tempered by selective constraints. Phylogenetic reconstruction showed a progressive relaxation of codon bias from algae to angiosperms while maintaining a conserved molecular economy cost of ~ 30 ATP per codon across the lineages. The study revealed codon usage bias is lineage-specific evolutionary conserved trait governed by mutation, selection, and translational optimization.

title: Spatial causal discovery reveals novel mechanisms of cellular senescence in human liver
summary: The complex network of mechanisms that surround cellular senescence, such as its precise causes and effects, are not entirely understood at present. Senescence occurs when a cell permanently ceases dividing, halts apoptosis, stops performing its normal functions, and begins secreting chemicals that can induce other cells in its environment to also become senescent. Senescent cells are present in both healthy and unhealthy tissue, but their abundance is positively correlated with disease and age. A better understanding of senescence could lead to healthier aging, improved recovery from chemotherapy, or increased lifespan. This study used novel machine learning algorithms - with guaranteed properties of correctness under broad assumptions - to investigate senescence in human liver tissue by analyzing Visium spatial transcriptomics data. This produced data-driven models of the causes and effects of senescence, both locally and from nearby tissue. This report includes an assessment of whether the data meet key requirements for causal analysis, the transcripts identified by causal analyses as causes and effects of senescence marker genes, and pathway analyses of those gene sets.

title: ProtFlap: Structure-based Deep Learning Prediction of Protein Flexibility from Atomic Energy Networks
summary: Protein flexibility is a key determinant of molecular recognition, catalysis, and regulation, yet remains difficult to characterise at scale. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations provide detailed descriptions of time-dependent dynamics but are computationally expensive. Although recent AI-based structure prediction methods have substantially improved access to high-quality static protein structures, they inherently lack information regarding the dynamic fluctuations essential for functional understanding. There is therefore a need for scalable, structure-based computational approaches that can infer intrinsic protein flexibility without explicit dynamical sampling. We present ProtFlap, a graph neural network framework for predicting relative residue-level flexibility directly from static protein structures. ProtFlap represents proteins as residue interaction graphs and integrates empirical atomic energy features extracted from a single energy-minimised snapshot with structural and sequence-derived descriptors. Central to our approach is the hypothesis that the local atomic energy network encoded in a frozen protein structure contains sufficient information to estimate structural flexibility. Trained using atomic mobility labels, quantified via normalised root-mean-square fluctuation (RMSF) derived from short MD simulations, ProtFlap achieves robust and accurate flexibility prediction across diverse protein domains. Feature attribution analysis reveals that van der Waals-related energy terms are the dominant contributors to the prediction.

title: Expansin couples salinity sensing to plant cell growth regulation
summary: In living plant cells, salt affects cell wall architecture directly and triggers diverse cellular responses that, in turn, feed back on wall organization and deposition. These intertwined effects obscure whether salt directly alters wall mechanical properties and thereby influences turgor-driven wall enlargement, the process underlying cell growth. In this study, we studied the tensile mechanical behavior of isolated cell wall materials at physiologically relevant salt concentrations. NaCl induced a small, reversible deformation without significantly altering the apparent axial tensile stiffness of hypocotyl walls. However, salt directly and reversibly inhibited acid-induced wall creep. Similar inhibition was observed in distinct cell wall types and in living Arabidopsis hypocotyls. Assays combining -expansin extracts with cellulose filter paper further supported direct inhibition of wall-loosening activity by salt. Molecular dynamics simulations suggested a mechanism in which Na electrostatically perturbs the conserved active-site Asp and its associated hydrogen-bond network. Together, these findings indicate that salt directly inhibits acid growth by suppressing -expansin-mediated wall creep, highlighting expansin as a physicochemical transducer linking environmental salinity to growth regulation.
